summary: Believable three-stream recycling station with good colour-coded hoods and labels, but plastic-box bodies, an odd rear and a lifted plinth keep it clearly CG.
critique: Proportions are close to a Glasdon Nexus-style trio (each unit roughly 0.6 m wide, about 1.2 m tall, sloped hood). The colour-coded hood tops (grey, blue, green), the three apertures (open square, letter slot, round glass hole), the door hinges and the vinyl labels with pictograms all read correctly. Problems: (1) The rear (opposite three-quarter) has a letter-slot opening in each back panel and the hoods are joined by small metal plates. Real units have blank backs, so this looks like the front aperture mirrored onto the back. (2) The bodies are one flat dark-grey colour with near-uniform roughness. Rotomoulded polyethylene has a soft satin sheen, slightly rounded vertical corners (R 15-25 mm), a moulded recessed door panel and a faint orange-peel texture, and none of that is present beyond a thin door outline. (3) The paper slot insert has a noisy dark pattern that reads as garbled text or moire at close range. (4) Only the top slope of each hood is coloured. On real Nexus units the whole hood moulding (sides and front lip) is the stream colour. (5) In the side view the base plinth looks lifted, with a dark gap and a hard shadow line, so the bin seems to hover. (6) Labels are crisp and centred but have vertical streak noise that looks like a filter, not weathering. There is no grime gradient at the base, no scuffs near the apertures and no drip stains under the hood lip.
suggestions: Remove the rear slots: back panels should be blank, perhaps with a moulded manufacturer logo emboss and two fixing bolts. Replace the metal joining plates with a hidden ganging bracket or a slim steel bar along the base.

Colour the full hood moulding (top, sides, front lip) in the stream colour (blue ~#2a62b8, green ~#3aa64c, grey ~#8a8f94). Bevel all hood and body vertical edges at 20 mm with 2-3 segments (about 200 extra tris per unit).

Body material: albedo ~#3a3d41, roughness 0.55-0.65 with a low-frequency mottled roughness map and a faint orange-peel normal (a tiled 256 px shared texture). Add a recessed door panel 5 mm deep with a 10 mm radius.
Plant the plinth: close the gap so the base meets the ground, and add an AO/contact-darkening strip on the bottom 80 mm with mud splash (vertex colour or a shared grime decal).
Replace the paper slot's noisy insert with a plain black rubber brush or flap strip (a simple dark material with vertical normal striations).

Weathering: grime under the hood overhang, hand-wear polish around the apertures, a few label edge lifts, faded label colours (desaturate 15%) and sticker residue. Use one shared 512 px wear atlas across all three units.
renderer_notes: The flat lawn and lack of GI exaggerate how floating the plinth looks. Contact shadows or AO would help, but the gap appears to be in the geometry too.

summary: A square slatted top on a single post reads as a garden table or stool, not a stadium bench plank. Clean but simplistic.
critique: The intent is stadium plank or bench seating, a long extruded aluminium or polymer seat plank on brackets fixed to a terrace riser. As a standalone module it reads as a small square table: the top is about as deep as it is wide, sits high on a single square tube post, and has no backrest. Side profile: the plank cross-section is four rounded ribs on a flat bar beam, so in the side view the planks float above a black cross-beam with a visible gap, which looks unsupported. The grey block bracket under one corner (the seat-number holder) is a plain box with no fixing detail. The seat number plate ('14') is good. The concrete footing pad and base plate with four nuts are nicely done. Materials: the plank is a uniform light grey with a fairly glossy, plastic look and no extrusion lines, anodised sheen, end caps or scuffs. The post is plain black with no galvanising or powder-coat texture. Scale is plausible for seat height (~0.45 m) only if the top is ~0.45 m square, but then the planks are far too deep for a single seat. Real seat depth is about 300-350 mm across 2-3 planks.
suggestions: Re-proportion as a real stadium bench run: a continuous plank 1.8-2.0 m long (four seat positions at 450-500 mm), seat depth 300-350 mm across 2-3 extruded slats, seat top at 430-450 mm above the tread.

Use two support brackets per run, at about 1/5 and 4/5 of the length, fixed to the riser face or tread with a short cantilevered arm, not a central pole on a concrete pad. If a freestanding version is needed, make it two legs with a T-foot.
Plank profile: extruded aluminium with rounded nose (R 15 mm), ribbed top (3-5 shallow grooves 3 mm deep), and moulded end caps in dark grey plastic. About 300 tris per run.

Material: anodised aluminium, albedo ~#b8bcc0, metallic 1, roughness 0.35 with a fine directional brushed normal along the length. Add scuffs on the nose and darker grime in the grooves (shared 512 px atlas). Seat numbers go on the plank nose every 450-500 mm as small stuck-on plates.
Brackets: galvanised steel, albedo ~#8d9196, roughness 0.5 with zinc spangle noise. Show bolts through the plank underside and the riser fixing.
renderer_notes: None. The issues are in proportions and construction.

summary: Overall dimensions are near a Golf-class hatch, but soft blobby surfacing, a long flat bonnet, no shut lines and matte paint make it look like a toy car.
critique: Measured from the side view, length-to-height (~0.35) and wheelbase-to-length (~0.64) are close to a Golf Mk8 (0.34, 0.615), and the wheels fill the arches well. The issues are form and surfacing. (1) The glasshouse is pushed back and the bonnet is long and nearly flat, so the profile reads as a shooting brake or crossover, not a modern hatch. On a Golf the A-pillar base sits roughly above the front axle plus ~0.5 m and the bonnet is short and steeply raked. (2) Body sides are soft, puffy extrusions with no shoulder crease, no sill line and no wheel-arch lips. The rear three-quarter view shows a lumpy discontinuity at the C/D-pillar. (3) There are no visible panel shut lines (doors, bonnet, tailgate, fuel flap) apart from faint seams. (4) The paint is matte, flat blue with no clear-coat reflection and no Fresnel highlight. (5) Glass is opaque dark blue-black with no reflection, no tint gradient and no visible interior silhouette at most angles. (6) The front fascia is a single bar of DRL across a smooth nose, with no real grille opening, fog lights or bumper cut lines. The plates (KD19 RVX white front, yellow rear) are correctly UK and help. (7) Mirrors are big blobs, and the black windscreen-scuttle trim strip is very prominent. Wheels (5-twin-spoke) and tyres are reasonable.
suggestions: Move the windscreen base forward about 250 mm and raise the bonnet's rear edge so the bonnet rakes down ~8-10 degrees to the nose. Shorten the visible bonnet to about 1.0 m. Keep overall L 4284 / W 1789 / H 1456 / WB 2636.

Add a crisp shoulder (tornado) line at about 0.85 m height running front to tail-light, a sill crease at about 0.30 m, and flared arch lips (20 mm proud). Silhouette edges need about 12-16 segments per arch. Budget about 8-12k tris for LOD0.
Cut shut lines as a 4 mm dark groove (geometry or a normal/AO decal) for four doors, bonnet, tailgate and fuel flap. Add door handles as small recessed bars.

Paint: metallic blue albedo ~#1f3f8a, metallic 0.0 base with a clear-coat layer (roughness 0.08 over base roughness 0.4). If clear-coat is unavailable, use roughness 0.2-0.25 so the sky reflects. Glass: roughness 0.05, dark tint, with Fresnel so it mirrors the sky at grazing angles.

Front: separate upper grille slot, lower intake with a honeycomb mesh decal, fog-lamp recesses and a number-plate recess. Rear: tailgate spoiler lip, rear-window wiper (present), bumper diffuser in textured black plastic (roughness 0.7).
Add dirt: road grime on the lower 200 mm and wheel arches, brake dust on the rims. One shared 1k vehicle wear texture can drive all hatch colour variants.
renderer_notes: No SSR or reflection probes makes all car paint and glass look flat. A cheap sky cube-map reflection would help a lot, but the paint roughness also needs lowering.

summary: A convincing generic green-and-yellow utility tractor with good lugged tyres, cab and beacon. Rear wheels are too small, and the paint wear is blotchy noise.
critique: This is a strong silhouette for a John Deere 6120M-type tractor: bonnet with grille, front weight block, exhaust stack beside the A-pillar, four-post glazed cab with a white roof, amber beacon, mirrors on arms, separate front mudguards, yellow rims and a rear linkage. Problems: (1) In the side view the rear tyre diameter is only about 1.3-1.4 m against a cab roof of about 2.9 m. A 600/65R38 rear is about 1.75 m and should reach well above the bonnet line and close to the cab floor-plus-0.8 m. The front tyres (540/65R24, ~1.25 m) look about right, so the front/rear ratio is too close to 1. (2) The bonnet is a simple rounded box. There are no side louvres, no bonnet split line, and the grille is a flat dark rectangle. (3) The cab glass shows no frame seals or door handle, and the rear window has no visible hinge. The cab roof is a plain slab without its moulded lip and work lights. (4) The paint wear is soft, cloudy, lighter-green blotches spread evenly over every panel (very visible in the close-up on the roof and bonnet). Real wear is mud and dust concentrated low, on mudguard undersides, steps and wheel rims, with the upper paint still glossy. (5) The paint is too matte and saturated for John Deere green, which is a fairly glossy enamel. (6) There are no steps or ladder to the cab door, no hydraulic hoses at the rear, no PTO guard and no rear work lights. The rear linkage is minimal. (7) The lugs read well in silhouette, but the tyre sidewalls lack lettering and bulge.
suggestions: Scale the rear wheels to ~1.75 m diameter, 0.6 m wide, and the fronts to ~1.25 m, 0.54 m wide. Raise the rear mudguards to match. Keep wheelbase 2.40-2.58 m and length 4.36 m.

Replace the cloudy paint blotches with directional grime: mud on the lower 0.5 m, inside the mudguards and on the rims, and dust on horizontal surfaces. Keep the upper paint glossy (roughness 0.25, albedo ~#367c2b). Yellow rims ~#f2c200 with brake-dust darkening at the hub.
Bonnet: add side louvre grilles (normal-mapped slots), a centre split line, a recessed headlight pair in the grille, and the grille as a mesh with depth (inset 30 mm).
Cab: rubber-sealed glass frames (black strip 20 mm), a door handle, a 2-3 rung step ladder below the door, two front and two rear roof work lights, and a moulded roof lip overhanging 60 mm.
Rear: three-point linkage with lift arms and top link, PTO shield, 2-4 coloured hydraulic coupler caps and a few hoses. About 1.5k tris.
Tyre sidewall: a shallow embossed lettering ring via normal map, and slight bottom bulge on the ground-contact side.
renderer_notes: The flat sky ambient makes the green paint read flat. Some of the lack of gloss may be the renderer, but the blotchy wear is in the texture.

summary: Recognisable bulrush (Typha) clump with cattail heads and mixed green/dry blades. Too sparse and ribbon-like to read as a real reed bed.
critique: The bulrush heads are correctly shaped (brown cylindrical spike with a thin tip above) and the mix of upright and arching blades with some dry straw-coloured leaves is right. Problems: (1) The clump is very sparse. A real Typha latifolia stand is a dense mass of 20-60 strap leaves per square metre, while here maybe 25-30 blades are spread over a wide footprint with large gaps, so it reads as a few grass cards. (2) The blades are flat ribbons of near-uniform width with no thickness, midrib or twist. Typha leaves are 10-25 mm wide, thick and spongy, slightly twisted, and taper sharply only at the tip. (3) The heads are a single flat reddish brown with no velvet texture. Real heads are dark chocolate brown (~#4a2e1c), velvety, and some burst into white fluff late in the season. (4) The muddy base patch is a flat decal with a hard edge. Reeds grow at water margins, so the base should be wet, darker and glossy, or the clump should sit at a water line. (5) Leaf colour is uniform mid-green with no blue-grey cast (Typha is distinctly glaucous) and no yellowing toward the tips. (6) Stem heights look about 1.5-2 m, which is fine.
suggestions: Triple the blade density in a tighter footprint (0.6-0.8 m radius): about 80-120 blades as alpha-free tapered quads with 4-6 segments each (~600-900 tris), or 12-16 crossed alpha cards with 8-10 blades each for a cheaper LOD.
Give each blade a V-fold cross-section (two triangles across, folded 20-30 degrees) and a gentle twist along its length. Width 15-20 mm, tapering in the top 15% only.

Leaf colour: glaucous green ~#6f8a5a to ~#86a06a with tips yellowing to ~#b9a46a. Back face slightly lighter, roughness 0.5, subtle translucency if supported. Make 20-30% of blades dead straw (~#c9b48a), concentrated at the outside and bending outward.
Heads: darker velvet brown ~#4a2e1c, roughness 0.9, a 10% chance of a fluffy, burst light-grey head, and a thin bare spike above each head (present; keep it).

Base: replace the flat mud decal with a soft-edged dark wet-soil patch (roughness 0.2-0.3, albedo ~#3b3226) with a few broken dead stems lying flat. Optionally ship a water-margin variant whose base is sunk under a water plane.
renderer_notes: Lack of translucency and GI makes the blades read darker inside the clump. That is renderer-side.

summary: A convincing bunded site diesel tank with dispenser cabinet, hazard signage and fittings. Saturated flat green, simple box construction and weak cabinet interior keep it below hero quality.
critique: It reads clearly as a steel bunded diesel tank (FuelSafe-type). The details are good: yellow 'DIESEL' labels, GHS pictograms (flammable, environmental hazard), a no-smoking sign, a data plate, a manway lid with bolt ring, a mushroom vent pipe, a fill point, lifting eyes at the top corners, skid runners underneath, and a hinged dispenser cabinet with meter, hose reel and nozzle. Problems: (1) The body is a plain box. Real bunded tanks have folded-steel rolled top edges, external stiffener ribs or channels on the long sides, and fork-lift pockets in the base skid. Here the side 'bands' are just lines. (2) The green is too saturated and uniform (lawn-like). Typical site tanks are RAL 6005 moss green (~#114232) or a duller ~#2e5a3a, with a semi-gloss powder coat. (3) The wear is long vertical rusty streaks applied evenly over every panel. Real wear is rust at the bottom edges and runners, scuffs on corners, and diesel drip stains under the cabinet and fill point. (4) The cabinet interior (side view) is mostly black. It needs a visible delivery hose coiled on a reel, a nozzle holster, a pump unit and a lockable hasp. (5) The open cabinet door has a heavy, slab-like panel with no inside frame. (6) Minor: the vent pipe is overly tall and thin compared with the squat tank, and the corner lifting eyes are tiny.
suggestions: Shift the albedo to RAL 6005-ish ~#1f4d32, roughness 0.4 semi-gloss with gentle orange-peel. Concentrate wear: rust bloom on the bottom 150 mm, skids and lifting eyes. Black diesel drips below the cabinet and fill cap. Edge chips on vertical corners only. Use a shared 1k wear atlas.
Geometry: add 2-3 pressed stiffening channels (50 mm deep) along each long side, a 40 mm rolled lip around the roof edge, and fork pockets (two 200 × 90 mm openings) in the base skid. About 600 tris.
Cabinet: a hose reel drum with 3-4 visible coils of black hose (simple torus segments), a nozzle on a holster bracket, a pump body box, an inside door frame lip, a padlock hasp and a door stay arm.
Shorten the vent to ~400 mm above the roof with a proper mushroom cap. Enlarge the lifting eyes to ~80 mm plates with a 40 mm hole.
Add a fill gauge or contents dial on top and a spill-kit decal or label on the cabinet face.
renderer_notes: The saturated grass background exaggerates how lawn-green the tank is, but the albedo is still too saturated in isolation.

summary: A good Glasdon Jubilee-style litter bin with dome hood, fluted body, gold band and crest. It is close to realistic, but the material is too uniform and small decal artefacts give it away.
critique: Shape and proportions match a Jubilee 110 well (about 1.16 m tall, ~0.6 m diameter, domed hood with a front aperture, gold band below the hood, fluted body, plinth). The aperture shows the liner and a cup inside, which is a nice touch. Problems: (1) The fluting on the body is very faint, so the body reads as a smooth tapered cylinder with vertical streak noise. Jubilee flutes are pronounced (about 15-20 mm deep), with crisp highlights. (2) Several small white 'H'/key-like marks on the side and back (lock indicators?) look like decal artefacts or missing textures at every distance. (3) The material is uniform satin dark grey. Real bins are black (~#1b1c1e), slightly glossy rotomoulded polyethylene, with sun-faded upper surfaces, white chewing-gum spots, sticker residue and grime around the aperture. (4) The gold band and crest are flat, unshaded yellow, with no gloss or slight relief. (5) The hood dome is smooth and perfect. Real units have a slight dome-to-collar transition ring and fixing bolts. (6) The base plinth is fine but meets the grass without any contact grime.
suggestions: Deepen the body flutes to 15-20 mm with 20-24 flutes around the circumference (geometry: 48-64 radial segments, ~1.5k tris), or keep the low-poly body and add a strong normal map. Flutes must catch the sun highlight.
Remove or fix the white 'H' marks. If they are the door lock, model a small recessed triangular-key lock (30 mm) in dark metal instead of a white decal.

Material: albedo ~#1c1d20, roughness 0.45 with low-frequency fading (upper surfaces ~10% lighter and rougher), gum spots (small light-grey dots on the lower half), a grime ring around the aperture lip and splash grime on the bottom 150 mm. Use a shared 512 px wear atlas.
Gold band: albedo ~#c9a227, roughness 0.3, raised 2 mm. Emboss the crest and LITTER lettering slightly (normal map) rather than flat paint.
Add the hood-to-body seam ring and two visible hinge or lock points at the back.
renderer_notes: The grass texture sharpening at the edges is renderer or lawn related, not the asset's fault.

summary: A convincing three-tier bowl with vomitories, aisles and fascias. The random tri-colour seat mosaic and repetitive, unshaded seat instances read as CG.
critique: Massing is impressive: three tiers with continuous LED fascias, aisle stairs with yellow nosings, vomitory openings, and a curved bowl that follows the pitch. Problems: (1) The seat colours are a random per-seat speckle of green, white and yellow that reads as noise or camouflage at every distance. Real stadiums use solid blocks of club colour, sometimes with a deliberate lettered or graphic pattern (the aerial view shows letters in the upper tier, which is good). Random scatter of individual off-colour seats is not realistic. (2) The seats are uniformly bright and flat. There is no darkening toward the back of each tier under the overhang, and no AO between rows, so the rows flatten out. (3) The vomitories are plain grey boxes protruding into the seating (seen in the lower-tier close views) with no handrails, side walls or signage. (4) The tier fronts and aisle steps lack handrails and glass balustrades on the upper tiers, which are required in real UK stands. (5) Concrete riser faces are invisible and seat rows look like a carpet. (6) There are no fans, stewards' positions, TV gantry or camera platforms and no press box, though those may be separate assets.
suggestions: Replace random per-seat colour with block patterns: a solid primary colour with 1-3% random fade variation, plus optional authored letter or stripe graphics. Drive this per section from a small low-res pattern texture sampled by seat position (zero extra geometry).
Add a per-row AO and shadowing term: darken seats by 30-50% toward the back of each tier under the overhang (bake into instance colour by depth under the upper tier).
Vomitories: model the side walls (concrete, 1.1 m high parapets) with a steel handrail on top, a dark tunnel void with soffit, and a section-number sign. About 300 tris each, instanced.
Handrails: tubular rails down every aisle (48 mm tube, a 0.9-1.1 m post every 2 m) and glass balustrades on the upper-tier fronts with a black top rail. Instanced, cheap.
Show riser faces: the concrete step face between rows (light grey ~#9a9a96, roughness 0.85) so rows read as stepped terrace.
renderer_notes: Without GI and AO, the deep rows under the roof get the same light as the front rows. A cheap baked vertical AO gradient would fix much of the flat look.

summary: A plausible full-ring cantilever roof with translucent panels and radial ribs. The underside framing is too regular and thin, and the top surface is a flat white plate.
critique: The roof forms a continuous oval ring with a central opening over the pitch. The underside shows radial rafters and a lattice of translucent panels, and the inner edge has hanging struts. From the aerial the roof top is clean white with radial seams, similar to a modern membrane or metal roof. Problems: (1) The underside structure is all the same thin grey members. Real cantilever roofs have deep primary trusses (2-5 m deep) with diagonals, secondary purlins and visible catwalks, lighting and speaker clusters. Here the structure reads as a shallow grid. (2) The translucent panels are uniform mid-grey with no light transmission variation. Polycarbonate panels glow brighter when sun-backlit. (3) The roof top is a flat slab with no gutter, no inner-edge compression ring, no fall, no drainage or maintenance walkways. Its leading edge is a simple thin lip. (4) The bottom-left overall view shows a huge flat grey slab under the roof edge ('NORTHWIND' on its lip) that reads as untextured geometry, likely a large screen or gantry back, and it dominates the shot. (5) There is no visible connection between the roof and the stand top (no columns, ties or back-span), so the cantilever seems to float.
suggestions: Model primary radial trusses every ~15 m as a triangular lattice (top chord, bottom chord 3-4 m below, diagonals), instanced around the ring (~400 tris each). Add a deep compression ring girder at the inner edge, about 2 m deep with diagonals.
Panels: a translucent material with brightness modulated by sun direction (cheap: an emissive term proportional to max(0, -dot(N, sun)) × 0.3) and alternating opaque metal panels near the back.

Roof top: add a 0.5 m gutter channel at the inner edge, radial standing-seam normal map and two maintenance walkways with handrails. Use slight panel albedo variation (±5%) and grime streaks running outward.

Fix the flat grey slab under the roof at the scoreboard end: either give it a proper structure (steel box-truss frame, access gantry, cladding with a panel normal) or reduce it to the actual screen housing.
Add back-span or support columns at the rear of the top tier, plus catwalks with lamp and speaker clusters on the underside.
renderer_notes: Without GI the underside of the roof and upper tier is lit as brightly as the sky side, which flattens the structure.

summary: A bold modern facade: gold vertical louvres over curtain-wall glazing between concrete stair cores. It looks good from a distance but is extruded and repetitive, with a bare plaza.
critique: The aerial and ground-distance views read as a real modern bowl stadium: vertical stair or lift cores at intervals, gold-yellow fin cladding on the upper half, glazed concourse levels below with floor bands, and a club sign high on a core. Problems: (1) The louvre fins are a uniform ripple that moirés at distance (noticeable aliasing in the detail view). Real fin cladding has visible fin depth, shadow between fins, and fixing rails or mullions every few metres. (2) The cores are plain concrete pylons with a column of small window dots, no doors at ground level, no turnstile blocks, no canopies and no signage (gate letters, club crest). (3) The glazing bands are uniform dark grey grids with no reflections, interior lights or concourse visible behind. (4) The ground plane is a flat light-grey slab with a few tiny trees. There are no turnstiles, ticket offices, kerbs, bollards, lighting columns or planters. At ground level the facade has no entrances. (5) The roof edge sits directly on the cladding with no visible soffit or fascia transition. (6) Scale cues are weak: the whole thing reads as an office drum because of the missing human-scale entrances.
suggestions: Give the fins real geometry or a strong normal and parallax with a dark gap between fins, varied fin angle (±10 degrees) per bay, and a horizontal fixing rail every 3 m. Add mip-aware filtering or a distance-based fade of fin frequency to kill moire.

Ground level: turnstile blocks (glazed booths with numbered gates) at each core, a steel entrance canopy, gate letters, a club crest on two cores, and ticket windows. All are reusable instanced modules.
Glazing: a reflective glass material (roughness 0.05) with an interior-mapping or emissive concourse layer showing lights and columns, so the facade is not a flat grid.
Plaza: a paving pattern texture with control joints, kerbs, a bollard line (security, 1.2 m spacing), lamp columns, bins and benches from the kit, and planters. Scatter more mature trees.
Add a roof-edge fascia or soffit 1-2 m deep in a contrasting metal (~#b8bcc0) where the roof overhangs the cladding.
renderer_notes: The louvre moire is partly texture filtering or the lack of TAA in the viewer, but the geometry density invites it.

summary: No legible floodlight installation: at most small grey struts at the roof's inner edge. A top-flight bowl needs a visible lamp ring or gantry.
critique: A mega bowl stadium with a full roof would normally carry its floodlights as a continuous ring of lamp clusters on a catwalk along the inner roof edge (as at Wembley, the Emirates and Tottenham). In these views the inner roof edge has only thin grey hanging members that read as structure, not luminaires. No lamp heads, reflector faces, lens glow or cabling are visible in any shot, including the roof-underside close-up. From the aerial no light gantry is visible on the roof lip. This element is effectively missing or illegible.
suggestions: Add an inner-edge lighting catwalk: a 1 m wide steel walkway with handrail along the compression ring, carrying lamp clusters every ~3 m (each about 0.6 × 0.5 × 0.3 m with a dark housing and a bright reflector face, ~100 tris instanced). A mega stadium needs about 300-400 heads in total.
Lamp material: housing ~#2a2c2e, roughness 0.5. Lens face: emissive white, with an off-state glass of light grey roughness 0.1. Aim all heads toward the pitch centre with per-cluster tilt variation.
Add cable trays, junction boxes and a few maintenance ladders on the catwalk for close-up shots.
Optionally add a few corner or sideline floodlight booms on the roof lip for broadcast-lighting variety.
renderer_notes: Lights are probably off in a daylight render, but the fittings should still be visible as objects.

summary: A strong pitch with mowing stripes, crisp markings, goalmouth wear and a believable goal with hex net. The best part of the stadium, but grass and lines are still too clean at mid-range.
critique: The pitch reads well: alternating mowing stripes, correct markings (centre circle, boxes, arcs), a worn sandy goalmouth patch, a corner flag, and a 3D ad carpet beside the goal. The goal frame is white with correct 7.32 × 2.44 m proportions, a hex-mesh net that is anti-aliased and visible against the stands, and back-stanchions. Problems: (1) At mid-range the turf is a uniform green with stripes but little colour variation. Real stadium turf shows subtle patch variation, slight yellowing at edges and in shade, and wear down the centre and along the linesman's run. (2) The line paint is pure bright white and perfectly uniform. Real lines have slightly broken edges and grass showing through. (3) The goal frame is a plain smooth tube with no elliptical or ogee profile and no net hooks, ground anchors or net-support elastic visible. The net hangs very regularly with no sag or slight bulge. (4) The goalmouth wear is a good start but is a flat colour blot. It should include worn divots and sand top-dressing. (5) The pitch-surround track or apron at the touchline is a plain dark strip. (6) The corner flag is tiny but fine.
suggestions: Turf: add a low-frequency (5-10 m) patch-variation texture modulating hue ±4% and brightness ±6%, plus a wear mask along the centre corridor, the goalmouth, and the assistant referees' running channel 1 m outside each touchline.
Lines: a 120 mm width with a noise-broken edge (±5 mm) and 85-90% paint opacity so grass shows through. Slightly off-white ~#f2f2ee.

Goal: use an elliptical tube profile (120 × 100 mm) with a slight bevel, net hooks every 0.3 m along posts and bar, and a net that sags 50-100 mm between the support points (vertex offset in the net shader or mesh). Add rear ground bar and pegs.
Goalmouth: combine the sand patch with a normal map of scuffed divots, and a darker damp ring in the six-yard box.
Apron: an artificial-grass apron in slightly bluer green, with a painted technical-area box and a few stewards' chairs.
renderer_notes: The large hard rectangular shadow on the pitch in the top-left view comes from the roof or screen geometry. It is plausible, but no penumbra or ambient occlusion makes it look stark.

summary: Correctly placed curved perspex dugouts either side of an arched tunnel, but they are simple, toy-like shells with flat green panels and no detail.
critique: The layout is right: two dugouts flanking a central player tunnel at halfway, each with rows of black seats under a curved green shell, and the tunnel with an arched extendable canopy. Problems: (1) The dugout shells are opaque flat green with no transparency. Real premium dugouts use tinted clear polycarbonate on an aluminium frame, so you see seats through them. (2) The seats are plain black blocks without padded bucket-seat detail (premium dugouts use padded car-style seats with headrests, often club coloured). (3) The tunnel mouth is a dark grey arch with two flat grey panels for doors. There is no depth, no lighting inside, no tunnel walls, signage or club branding. (4) The extendable tunnel canopy (seen in the detail view) is a green ribbed arch with good shape but no concertina folds or wheels. (5) There is no technical-area markings detail (present faintly), no fourth-official board, and no water-bottle crates or equipment.
suggestions: Dugout shells: tinted clear polycarbonate (roughness 0.1, 60-70% opacity, slight blue-grey tint) on a brushed aluminium frame (40 mm tube) with a solid club-colour back panel to 1 m height. Embed a club crest decal on the side glass.
Seats: padded bucket seats with headrest (~250 tris each, instanced), in club colour or black leatherette with roughness 0.5 and stitching normal map.
Tunnel: model 3-4 m of tunnel depth with lit walls (emissive ceiling strip), a club-crest wall graphic, and floor in rubber matting. The door panels should be pushed back into the void.
Extendable canopy: concertina folds every 0.6 m (sawtooth profile), a white or club-colour fabric material with slight sag, and small castor wheels at each frame hoop.
Add a fourth-official desk, an electronic substitution board on a stand, and drinks crates as instanced props near the technical area.

summary: Rich, varied sponsor branding on ribbon fascias, perimeter boards and a 3D carpet, plus a readable scoreboard. Flat, uniformly lit panels and a crude screen housing keep it CG.
critique: This is strong for density and believability: 360-degree LED ribbon fascias on two tier fronts carrying many fictional brands (Meridian Tyres, Kestrel Bank, Halcyon, Volta, Northwind, Summit Cola), pitchside boards with good graphic design and taglines, a 3D carpet by the goal, and a scoreboard showing 'KIT FC 2 - 1 ROVERS' with the match clock. Problems: (1) The LED boards render as matte printed panels. Real LED perimeter and ribbon boards are emissive, saturated and slightly glowing, with a visible pixel grid at close range and a dark bezel or frame. (2) The perimeter boards have flat fronts with no visible bracket or frame structure or angled back, and the board tops are clean white edges. (3) The main scoreboard is a flat dark rectangle with simple text and no bezel, mounting frame or supporting steel. Its rear (bottom-left overall view) appears as a large blank grey slab. (4) The ribbon fascias repeat the same brand sequence in a short loop, so repetition is obvious around the bowl. (5) The board graphic text is sharp and clean but small taglines blur. Fine for distance.
suggestions: Make LED surfaces emissive (intensity 1.5-3× albedo) with a subtle pixel-grid normal or modulation visible within 10 m, and a 20 mm black bezel around each panel.
Perimeter boards: a 0.9 m tall board with a 10-15 degree back-lean, a black steel A-frame visible from behind, and cable runs. Add a foam padding strip on top for the pitch-facing side.

Scoreboard: a 300 mm deep black bezel frame, a steel truss support visible above or behind, and a clad rear housing with service doors instead of the flat slab. Add a club crest and a sponsor strip under the screen (present; keep it).
Ribbon board content: randomise the sponsor order per section and add animated or rotating content offsets per instance so the sequence doesn't visibly repeat.
Add a second screen at the opposite end for a stadium of this size.
renderer_notes: Lack of bloom and emissive support makes LEDs look printed. A simple emissive term plus bloom would lift them a lot.
